change.requirement_text:
# Requirement #2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack

I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as `[IsExternalInit]` or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using `IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput` instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

plants.description: The walk up the base-type chain is disabled, so only members declared directly on the formatted type are collected. Inherited public read-write members are silently omitted from the generated formatter, causing data loss on round-trip.

The class check is inverted, so the deserializing-constructor validation is skipped for classes (and applied to structs instead). A class with no accessible parameterless constructor now passes validation and the generated formatter fails to compile.
Contractless mode no longer collects any members, so a formatter generated without a surrogate serializes an empty object and the feature is effectively unusable for types from a referenced assembly.
[IgnoreMember] on surrogate members is no longer honoured, so members the user explicitly excluded are either serialized or cause the whole collection to fail with a MemberNeedsKey diagnostic.

The int-keyedness discovered from the surrogate's [Key] attributes is discarded and always reported as false, so a surrogate with integer keys produces a formatter that writes string keys instead of the declared integer keys.
Local variable renamed from targets to candidates; no behavioural change.
Equivalent rewrite of the first-location lookup using a length check and indexer instead of FirstOrDefault().
The memberIsIntKey temporary is inlined; the resulting key-kind logic is identical.

The GeneratedFormatterMustImplementFormatter descriptor is given the id constant of the 'must be partial' diagnostic, so two descriptors share id MsgPack019 and the MsgPack020 diagnostic is never emitted. Suppressions and error codes for the 'must implement IMessagePackFormatter<T>' rule become wrong/ambiguous.

plants.description: Replaces the implicitly typed loop variable with its explicit type; no behavioural change.

findings.message: Surrogate member type matching is not validated. CreateSurrogateMembers matches a surrogate member to a formatted-type member by name only (and checks public read-write accessibility), but never verifies that the member types are identical. The MsgPack022 diagnostic is documented as requiring 'same name and type', and the test SurrogateMemberMustHaveMatchingType expects it when a surrogate declares string Id against an int Id on the formatted type, but the diagnostic will not be reported because the type comparison is missing.

GetInstanceMembers never walks the inheritance hierarchy: the for-loop increment is `current = null`, so the loop body runs only for the formatted type itself and base-type members are never enumerated. The comment claims base types are included, but they are not. This causes inherited public read-write instance members to be omitted in contractless mode, and prevents surrogate members from matching inherited members of the formatted type. The increment should be `current = current.BaseType`.

The parameterless-constructor check applies to all non-class types, including structs. For structs, InstanceConstructors typically does not include the implicit parameterless constructor, so structs without explicit constructors (such as ExternalPoint in the tests) are incorrectly rejected with NoDeserializingConstructor. This contradicts the requirement that 'any struct can be created without one.' The check should only apply to classes (change !isClass to isClass, or skip structs entirely).

Contractless mode does not serialize any members. When surrogate is null, Collect sets members to Array.Empty<MemberSerializationInfo>() instead of calling CreateContractlessMembers(type). The CreateContractlessMembers method exists but is never invoked, so a generated formatter for a type without a surrogate would serialize nothing, making the primary feature (contractless serialization of external types) non-functional.

CreateSurrogateMembers does not skip surrogate members marked with [IgnoreMember]. It requires every instance member of the surrogate to have a [Key] attribute with an int or string value. A member with [IgnoreMember] but no [Key] triggers MemberNeedsKey and causes generation to return null. This contradicts the documented behavior (README.md and MsgPack022.md show [IgnoreMember] used without [Key]) and breaks the provided test ExternalWidgetSurrogate, which has [IgnoreMember] on Internal without [Key].

isIntKey is unconditionally set to false before returning, overriding the key-kind detection performed earlier in CreateSurrogateMembers. When a surrogate uses integer keys, the formatter will be configured with isIntKey=false, causing string keys to be used on the wire while the surrogate declares integer keys, leading to serialization/deserialization mismatches.

The diagnostic reporting pipeline for [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] does not iterate over the generated formatter requests. It accesses s.Left.Left.Formatter and s.Left.Left.Surrogate on the collection/tuple itself rather than on each GeneratedFormatterRequest item, so diagnostics for invalid generated formatters (non-partial, missing IMessagePackFormatter<T>, unsupported data type, surrogate mismatches) are never reported. Users get a silent failure: no model is generated and no diagnostic is produced.

Invokes MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.NoDeserializingConstructor, but this descriptor is not shown in the SupportedDiagnostics list in the diff. If it is not already registered in the analyzer, the diagnostic will be silently dropped and the compiler will not report the missing constructor issue.

refused_to_decide: Whether MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.NoDeserializingConstructor is already defined in SupportedDiagnostics (not visible in the diff). If it is not, the diagnostic at GeneratedFormatterCollector.cs line 79 will not be reported.

findings.message: The template emits a class declaration ("partial class ... : IMessagePackFormatter<T>") for user-declared formatters, but it does not include the accessibility modifier from the user's declaration. The generator should either omit the class declaration for user-declared formatters and emit only the method bodies, or emit the accessibility from INamedTypeSymbol.DeclaredAccessibility.

# Requirement #2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack

I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add an assembly-level attribute `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatterFor]` that can be applied multiple times in Project B, naming types from referenced assemblies. The source generator will emit a formatter class for each named type automatically, without requiring the user to declare any partial formatter class.

For example:

```csharp
[assembly: GeneratedMessagePackFormatterFor(typeof(ProjectA.MyType))]
```

That's it. The generator creates the formatter implementation and registers it in the generated resolver. No user-declared `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` class is needed.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as `[IsExternalInit]` or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using `IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput` instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

findings.message: The requirement asks for an assembly-level attribute [GeneratedMessagePackFormatterFor] that can be applied multiple times in Project B, naming types from referenced assemblies, and generating a formatter automatically without requiring the user to declare any partial formatter class. The PR instead adds a class-level attribute [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] that must be placed on a user-declared partial formatter class, and the user must still declare the class and implement IMessagePackFormatter<T>. This does not implement the requested feature; it implements a different design where the generator only fills in the body of a formatter the user must already write.

The collector requires the formatter class to be partial and to implement IMessagePackFormatter<T> (diagnostics MsgPack019-MsgPack022). This enforces the user-declared partial class pattern that the requirement explicitly says should not be necessary. The generator should be able to emit a formatter for a named type from a referenced assembly without any user-declared formatter class.

The source generator wires up [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] on class declarations, not an assembly-level attribute. There is no code path that discovers types from referenced assemblies and generates formatters for them automatically, which is the core of the requirement.
